content.title: About
content.content: Cappuccino is an espresso topped with a thick layer of milk foam. In this version non‑dairy milk (soy, oat, almond, etc.) is used, making the drink suitable for those avoiding dairy. It offers a smooth, creamy taste with a subtle coffee bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “cappuccino” comes from the Italian word for “little capuchin”, referring to the drink’s colour resembling the robes of Capuchin monks.
The first cappuccino was created in Italy in the early 20th century.
Plant‑based milks lower the saturated‑fat and lactose content compared with cow’s milk.
In many countries cappuccino is served with a sprinkle of cinnamon or cocoa powder.
Cappuccino often serves as a base for flavored versions such as vanilla, caramel, or mint.

items.title: Stimulating caffeine effect
items.content: The espresso provides caffeine, which can improve alertness and concentration.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Non‑dairy milks usually contain less saturated fat than dairy milk, supporting heart health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from plant milk
items.content: Soy and oat milks are often fortified with calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Some plant milks contain probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: High caffeine intake may cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to soy, oat, or almond milk.

items.title: Added sugar in flavored versions
items.content: Pre‑flavored cappuccinos often contain added sugars, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain drugs, such as CNS stimulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cappuccino is served hot in ceramic cups, often garnished with cinnamon, cocoa powder, or chocolate shavings. Sweeteners can be added to taste. Choose a plant‑based milk without animal‑derived additives for a vegan option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared cappuccino is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours; re‑heat and re‑foam before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain crackers are crunchy biscuits made from a blend of whole grains, seeds, and sometimes nuts. They have a rich nutty‑grain flavor with a light salty note and work well as a snack on their own or as a base for toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Typical grain mix includes wheat, oats, rye, barley and sunflower seeds.
Multigrain crackers often contain more dietary fiber than white bread.
Flavor variations range from flaxseed and pumpkin seed to dried tomato and herb blends.
They are popular in diet plans because they pair easily with low‑calorie spreads.
In many countries they are served with cheese and ham as a classic appetizer.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The whole‑grain blend provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Grains supply thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Seeds such as sunflower and flax add polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Crackers provide magnesium, iron and zinc, supporting muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Most crackers contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are heavily salted; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Although light, crackers still contribute calories; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Flavored versions may contain sugar or honey, which can be problematic for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy crackers straight from the pack, spread with cottage cheese, hummus, avocado, or use as a base for canapés with cheese and vegetables. They also add a pleasant crunch when tossed into soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Cucumber (Cucumis sativus) is an annual herbaceous plant of the gourd family cultivated for its edible fruit. Raw cucumbers have a refreshing, mildly sweet flavor, a crisp texture, and a high water content (about 95 %). They are eaten fresh, in salads, as snacks, and as an ingredient in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cucumbers are composed of almost entirely water, making them an excellent way to stay hydrated.
They contain antioxidants such as vitamin C, beta‑carotene, and flavonoids.
There are over 100 cucumber varieties differing in shape, color, and taste.
Cucumbers can be grown in open fields, greenhouses, and hydroponic systems.
The word “cucumber” derives from the Latin “cucumis,” meaning “a herbaceous fruit.”

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: Cucumbers are low in calories (about 15 kcal per 100 g), making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: They provide vitamin K, vitamin C, potassium, and magnesium, supporting bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidant Properties
items.content: Flavonoids and tannins in cucumbers help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Fiber in the skin promotes healthy digestion and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cucumbers, resulting in skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Pesticide Residues
items.content: Non‑organic cucumbers may carry pesticide residues; it is advisable to wash them thoroughly before eating.

items.title: Digestive Issues
items.content: People with irritable bowel syndrome may experience gas and bloating from cucumbers due to fermentable carbs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cucumbers are eaten raw, sliced into salads, with dips, or as a snack. They can be added to smoothies, juices, and cold soups such as gazpacho. Keeping the skin is recommended, as it holds most of the nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cucumbers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel or a perforated bag. When stored properly they keep for 5‑7 days. Avoid storing them near ethylene‑producing fruits, which accelerate spoilage.

egg-yolk-only-cooked-ns-as-to-fat.title: Egg, yolk only, cooked, NS as to fat

content.title: About
content.content: The cooked egg yolk is the nutrient‑dense part of the egg, containing most of its fats, vitamins, and minerals. When boiled, the yolk firms up but retains the majority of its nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yolk holds almost all of the egg’s nutrients, including vitamins A, D, E, K and the B‑complex.
Cooked yolk is easier to digest than raw yolk.
Although yolk is a source of cholesterol, current research shows moderate intake does not raise blood cholesterol for most people.
Yolk contains lecithin – a natural emulsifier beneficial for liver and brain health.
Boiling preserves nearly all of the yolk’s antioxidants.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and promotes bone health.

items.title: Contains lecithin
items.content: Lecithin helps liver function and supports normal nervous system activity.

items.title: High in biotin
items.content: Biotin (vitamin B7) is important for carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron and selenium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and antioxidant protection.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Consuming large amounts of yolk may raise cholesterol levels in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to egg whites or yolks.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Overconsumption can lead to vitamin A toxicity, especially in pregnant women.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked yolk can be eaten on its own, added to salads, pâtés, sauces, or used as a filling for sandwiches. It can also be mashed and mixed with vegetables for a nutrient‑rich snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled yolks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Ham or pork salad is a ready‑to‑eat dish made of diced ham or boiled pork, fresh vegetables (cucumber, tomato, onion), hard‑boiled eggs and a dressing based on mayonnaise or sour cream. Herbs and spices are often added. It works well as a light lunch or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham salad is popular in Eastern Europe and the United States as a quick picnic dish.
The ham used can be smoked, boiled or baked, each giving a different flavor profile.
Traditional recipes include hard‑boiled eggs, which add a creamy texture.
The salad is often served in individual glasses or on lettuce leaves for easy portioning.
A vegetarian version replaces ham with tofu or smoked mushrooms.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Ham and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Ham is a source of iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Vegetables
items.content: Fresh veggies add vitamin C, fiber and antioxidants.

items.title: Convenient meal
items.content: The combination of protein and vegetables makes the salad a nutritious, quickly digestible option.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains a lot of salt, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork and ham can be high in saturated fat, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to certain meats.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage of the prepared salad can lead to bacterial growth, especially above 4 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, as a standalone dish, a side, or in sandwiches. It keeps well in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Before serving you can add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon or a dash of mustard to brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the fridge at 0‑4 °C. Do not leave it at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Check for off‑odors or changes in texture before eating; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Mutton is the meat of mature sheep, usually older than one year, with a deep red color, firm texture, and a stronger, richer flavor than lamb. It is widely eaten in Central Asia, the Middle East, South Asia, and parts of Europe and Africa. Mutton is traditionally slow-cooked, stewed, roasted, or grilled and is used in dishes such as pilaf, curries, stews, and kebabs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mutton comes from adult sheep, while lamb comes from sheep under one year old.
It has a stronger, gamier flavor than lamb because of the animal's age.
Mutton is a staple meat in Central Asia, the Middle East, and South Asia.
It is well suited to slow cooking, which makes tough cuts tender.
Mutton fat has a distinctive flavor and a firm texture at room temperature.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Mutton provides complete protein for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Rich in heme iron
items.content: Mutton contains iron that the body absorbs readily.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides selenium and niacin
items.content: These nutrients support antioxidant defenses and energy metabolism.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Mutton can be high in saturated fat, especially fatty cuts, so choose leaner cuts and trim visible fat.

items.title: Red meat consumption
items.content: Health organizations generally suggest limiting red meat, especially processed meat, because high intakes are linked to some health risks.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked mutton can carry harmful bacteria. Cook whole cuts to at least about 63 °C (145 °F) and let them rest, and ground mutton to about 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Purines and cholesterol
items.content: Mutton contains purines and cholesterol, which matters for people with gout or certain heart-related conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mutton is best cooked slowly with moisture, such as braised, stewed, or simmered in pilaf, soups, and curries, or marinated and grilled as kebabs. Trim excess fat before cooking, and pair mutton with vegetables, whole grains, and herbs. Marinating in yogurt, lemon, or spices helps tenderize it.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw mutton in the coldest part of the refrigerator and cook it within three to five days, or ground mutton within one to two days. Freeze it for longer storage and thaw it in the refrigerator. Cooked mutton should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days.

pizza-with-cheese-and-extra-vegetables-m.title: Pizza with cheese and extra vegetables, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with cheese and extra vegetables on a medium crust is a classic Italian dish made with a thin dough base, tomato sauce, melted mozzarella cheese, and a variety of fresh vegetables such as bell peppers, mushrooms, onions, olives, and tomatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A medium crust typically measures about 0.5–0.7 cm in thickness, offering a balance between a crisp edge and a soft interior.
Mozzarella cheese traditionally comes from water buffalo milk, but most commercial pizzas use cow's milk mozzarella.
Adding vegetables boosts the content of vitamins A, C, and K as well as dietary fiber.
Pizza gained widespread popularity in the United States after World War II when American soldiers brought the recipe back from Italy.
A standard medium pizza usually weighs 300–350 g, making it a convenient single serving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Mozzarella cheese and vegetables provide essential amino acids needed for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables supply vitamin C, potassium, and antioxidants that support immune function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetables and whole‑grain crust (if used) increase fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with meat‑topped pizzas, this version contains less saturated fat, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables have high water content, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Mozzarella contains lactose, which may cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dairy proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese can be salty; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crust contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite the vegetables, pizza can be calorie‑dense due to cheese and crust; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cutting it into 6–8 slices. Fresh basil or arugula can be added after baking for extra aroma. Optionally drizzle a little olive oil or balsamic glaze.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, cooked, NFS (Not From Specification) is a ready‑to‑eat rice prepared without added salt, fats, or flavorings. It retains the natural taste and nutritional profile of the grain, providing a convenient source of carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooked rice is a staple in many diet plans because it is naturally low in fat.
The NFS label indicates the product does not conform to any specific food specification, offering flexibility for various culinary uses.
Rice feeds more than half of the world’s population.
Most vitamins of the B‑complex are retained when rice is cooked without draining the water.
There are over 40,000 rice varieties, though most commercial products are based on aromatic types like basmati and jasmine.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice is rich in complex carbohydrates that provide sustained energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooked rice contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Provides magnesium, phosphorus and small amounts of iron, supporting muscle and bone health.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: Rice rarely triggers food allergies, making it safe for most individuals.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice has a high GI, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: White cooked rice is low in dietary fiber, so it should be paired with vegetables or whole‑grain foods.

items.title: Arsenic presence
items.content: Rice grown in some regions may contain arsenic; choose reputable brands to minimize exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked rice can be served as a side dish, added to salads, soups, sushi, or used as a base for meals with vegetables and protein. It reheats well in the microwave or on a skillet with a splash of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C; reheat thoroughly after thawing.
